title: The First Counterattacks
subtitle: Counterattacks, broken communications and the widening northern war
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Soviet armour delayed German formations in Lithuania and Ukraine, but shortages and broken communications prevented local attacks from becoming a coordinated recovery of the front.
body:
An attack timed to the hour

Colonel Poluboyarov, head of the Northwestern Front’s armoured administration, sent his report on 23 June. Timed 5:50 a.m., it records a counterattack being assembled through personal intervention in a failing communications system. He had visited Alexey Kurkin and the 8th Army commander, ordered Kurkin to attack at noon, and intended to require Nikolai Shestopalov to begin an hour earlier. He was still leaving to reach Shestopalov’s corps. The army charged with coordination had contact with neither front headquarters nor the corps. His requests for aircraft, fuel and ammunition identified what the counterattack still lacked. By 25 June, that gap between issuing a plan and assembling the means to execute it had become central to the Soviet effort in Lithuania and western Ukraine. [1]

The same problem confronted Soviet resistance across much of the invaded frontier. The Red Army was counterattacking, sometimes with determination and considerable local force. It was not standing aside while German columns passed. But attacking formations had to find the enemy, reach their assembly areas and cooperate with neighbours whose whereabouts were uncertain. German commanders could therefore encounter a dangerous tank attack on one road while another formation continued advancing beyond it. The Soviet difficulties were organizational and physical as well as tactical: a tank that could defeat an opposing vehicle could still become useless for want of fuel, a passable crossing or an order that reached its crew in time. [2]a

The fighting around Raseiniai illustrates that distinction particularly well. Here the Soviet command tried to strike the flank of Army Group North’s advance and protect the retreat of its rifle formations. The attack imposed a real battle on German armoured troops, but it did not restore the front. In western Ukraine, a larger concentration of Soviet mechanized corps was still developing its own counterstroke. Meanwhile, the war was becoming open and unmistakable in Finland, and German conquest in Lithuania was already bringing organized anti-Jewish violence. These were connected developments, although they cannot be reduced to a single narrative of tanks racing east. [3]

Read the dated map alongside the Soviet orders and reports. The orders specify intended movements; the reports describe missing units, broken communications and shortages. Together they show the problem behind the counterattacks: scattered Soviet formations had to converge before German columns could exploit the gaps between them. Neither source provides a complete account of control over every intervening locality.[4]b

The roads through Lithuania

Field Marshal Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb’s Army Group North had three principal instruments. Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army advanced on the Baltic side; Ernst Busch’s 16th Army operated farther inland; Erich Hoepner’s 4th Panzer Group supplied the mobile striking force between and ahead of them. Its two motorized corps followed different routes. Georg-Hans Reinhardt’s XLI Corps encountered the Soviet armour around Raseiniai and the Dubysa, while Erich von Manstein’s LVI Corps drove farther east toward the Western Dvina crossing at Daugavpils, also called Dvinsk. Their common purpose was to break the Soviet armies in the Baltic region and open the approach toward Leningrad. Their immediate experiences were already diverging. [5]

The rivers explain much of the operational geometry. The Niemen lay near the opening battlefield; the Dubysa divided routes through central Lithuania; the Western Dvina offered a much larger defensive barrier farther northeast. German success depended on crossing these obstacles before Soviet forces could organize behind them. Soviet success required more than the survival of a bridgehead or a single division. It required withdrawing troops to reach a new line, headquarters to establish communications and reserves to arrive before the attackers converted a crossing into a route for their whole formation. Roads and bridges made that a race with a limited number of possible destinations. [5]c

Fyodor Kuznetsov commanded the Soviet Northwestern Front. Pyotr Sobennikov’s 8th Army covered the northwestern part of the threatened area, with Vasily Morozov’s 11th Army farther south. Their deployment had already been disrupted by the initial German blows. Kuznetsov’s directive of 22 June identified the German penetration toward Tauragė as a threat to the 8th Army and ordered the 3rd and 12th Mechanized Corps to intervene. The 12th was to turn against the flank and rear of the advancing Germans. The 3rd was to bring its 2nd Tank and 84th Motorized Divisions toward Raseiniai, while leaving its 5th Tank Division with the 11th Army. That qualification matters: the 3rd Corps was not entering this battle with all the formations listed under its name in a prewar inventory. [6]

The order also assigned Sobennikov responsibility for coordinating the two corps and directed the air force to strike German concentrations. This was a combined operation in conception, with armour, aviation, antitank defence and the retreating infantry intended to support one another. Its weakness lay in the widening distance between that conception and the actual condition of the command system. The same directive was trying to prevent encirclement, arrange a counterattack and prepare positions east of the Niemen. Headquarters was already pursuing several urgent tasks with forces whose freedom of movement was shrinking. [6]d

Raseiniai and the broken counterstroke

Poluboyarov’s report gives the counterstroke a more precise shape than the broad arrows usually drawn over Lithuania. Kurkin’s 3rd Mechanized Corps was to move west from Raseiniai toward the Tauragė–Šiauliai road, then turn southwest toward Tauragė and Tilsit. Shestopalov’s 12th Corps was to advance southwest on the other side of that road. The intention was to bring converging pressure against the German penetration rather than send tanks forward wherever fighting could be heard. Poluboyarov had arranged a coded coordination table and sought attacks at eleven and noon on 23 June. His departure to find the 12th Corps shows that part of this coordination was still an intended personal intervention. [1]

The request for aircraft and fuel shows how much remained unsettled behind those exact hours. The army responsible for directing the two corps had lost contact with both. His visit could deliver a task to one commander; it could not ensure that the other corps, its fuel columns and its supporting aircraft would arrive in step. This was a plan being held together by personal journeys through a front that German troops were continuing to break. [1]

Around Raseiniai, Soviet heavy tanks made that incomplete attack tactically formidable. The German 6th Panzer Division encountered vehicles against which some of its customary antitank weapons were inadequate. German battle groups had to combine heavier guns, manoeuvre and close action instead of assuming that their normal armament would settle every encounter. The best-known episode, examined in Arvydas Žardinskas’s archival research, concerned a single KV tank and a road the division needed to keep open. [7]e

A famous encounter

One tank and the scale of a claim

For about a day, one KV blocked the Raseiniai–Šiluva road and interrupted contact between two battle groups of the 6th Panzer Division. Žardinskas’s English abstract describes repeated German attempts to eliminate it. That was a consequential local action. It did not stop the German formations advancing on other routes.[7]f

The Soviet evening summary for 24 June is more revealing about the wider battle than any isolated duel. It claimed a major success for the 2nd Tank Division, including large German equipment losses, but also reported that the division was around Raseiniai without fuel. German reserves had arrived and were attacking. The front was considering delivering fuel by aircraft. The same report said that the effect of the 12th Mechanized Corps’ operations could not be felt and blamed Shestopalov’s inactivity. These are statements by an embattled headquarters, not findings from an impartial inquiry. The German losses cannot simply be accepted as audited totals, and the accusation against the commander must be read beside the earlier admission that communications were broken. [2]

The fuel shortage explains why the heavy tanks’ local effect could not be sustained. A division unable to replenish could neither repeat its attacks nor withdraw all its vehicles when German forces threatened its routes. Meanwhile, the failure to coordinate the two corps left the Germans able to concentrate against one threat while advancing elsewhere. Difficult encounters recorded by German units and defeat reported by Soviet headquarters describe different levels of the same battle. The tanks’ resistance was real; the system needed to keep them fighting was failing. [2] [4]g

A retreat that could not move as one

The Northwestern Front’s reports show that the tank battle was only one part of a larger disintegration. On the Baltic coast, the 67th Rifle Division was fighting around Liepāja, called Libau in German records. The front reported heavy fighting, bombing of the harbour, airfield and railway station, fires in the city and the loss of communications. Farther inland, units of the 11th Army had lost much of their equipment and were attempting to reorganize around Babtai, Jonava and Vepriai. The whereabouts of the 128th Rifle Division were unknown to front headquarters. Each of these statements describes a different condition; none can be represented adequately by saying that the Northwestern Front had simply vanished. [2]

The report also followed a German motorized column moving toward Šiauliai after a breakthrough between Kražiai and Kelmė between 7 and 8 p.m. on 24 June. That direction threatened the connections behind the Soviet troops fighting around Raseiniai. Elsewhere in the same army, part of the 11th Rifle Division was organizing a new defensive line while the rest had yet to arrive from Narva. The problem was therefore not only replacing losses suffered in battle. A commander might be expected to defend a position with a formation whose remaining components were still approaching from far away, while an enemy column was already turning the roads behind it into a battlefield. [2]h

Desertion also contributed to the breakdown. One documented example concerns troops recently absorbed from a state the Soviet Union had occupied. Aleksandr Čapenko’s study of the Lithuanian 29th Territorial Rifle Corps links arrests of former Lithuanian officers and the June deportations to weakened discipline and growing hostility to Soviet rule. He reports that the corps failed to cover Vilnius on 23 June, became encircled and suffered substantial desertion. A Soviet decision of 25 June called for the territorial corps to be withdrawn east for reconstitution, citing depleted strength and political unreliability. This evidence concerns a particular formation with a coercive history of incorporation. It does not turn every missing soldier into a deserter: combat losses, separation and escape from encirclement also reduced effective strength. Nor does it establish one motive for every man who left. [8]i

While Reinhardt’s corps fought around Raseiniai, Manstein’s advanced towards the Western Dvina. The withdrawing Soviet armies needed to reach that river and organize its defence before German mobile forces took the crossings. Resistance on one route could delay a German formation without winning that wider race.[5]j

The larger armoured battle forming in Ukraine

Farther south, the counterattack problem appeared on a greater scale. Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South was advancing with Ewald von Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group, supported by Walter von Reichenau’s 6th Army on the northern part of the sector and Carl Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army farther south. Mikhail Kirponos’s Southwestern Front possessed substantial mechanized forces, but their locations, movements and changing assignments prevented them from becoming a single concentrated weapon at the moment of the German crossing. The geography of Lutsk, Dubno, Brody and the approaches from Lwów created opportunities to strike the German penetration from different directions. It also created long and congested routes along which those forces first had to arrive. [9]

Kirponos’s order issued at Tarnopol at nine on the evening of 24 June specified an attack at seven the following morning. The 8th, 15th and 4th Mechanized Corps were named in the intended operation, which was to defeat the German mobile grouping north of the Shchurovytse–Dmytriv–Mosty Velyki line and reach the Voynytsia–Mylatyn–Sokal area. One purpose was to avert the encirclement of Mikhail Potapov’s 5th Army. The order required units to occupy their starting positions during the night and commanders to verify that subordinates understood their tasks. These were concrete instructions with a date and an hour, not a vague exhortation to counterattack. [10]

The aviation arrangements were equally exact on paper. Reconnaissance was to identify targets before 6.50; the strongest opening air strike was to take place in the ten minutes before seven; successive attacks were to support the armour afterward. Tanks would mark themselves with red rockets and folded white sheets, and aircraft would signal recognition by rocking a wing. Such details reveal both a serious effort at cooperation and the fragility of the methods available. A timetable this precise depended on formations arriving together, pilots finding the intended targets and tank units distinguishing friendly aircraft while already under pressure. [10]

By late on 25 June, a new order prescribed another attack for the next morning. The 8th and 15th Mechanized Corps were again central, now joined in the wider design by the 9th and 19th under Potapov’s control southwest of Lutsk. Assembly was required by 4.30 and the attack by nine on 26 June. The target was the German grouping around Radekhiv, and the northern corps were to assist by attacking along the Lutsk–Brody railway. This revised program is direct evidence that the intended result of the previous order had not been secured on its stated terms. It does not establish that nothing had happened on 25 June; it establishes that the desired coordinated defeat of the German force remained ahead rather than behind. [11]k

Cooperation prescribed in detail

Sheets, rockets and a missing map

Southwestern Front order 0015 of 24 June prescribed red rockets and folded white sheets to identify tanks to supporting aircraft, with aircraft signalling by rocking a wing. The published collection also notes that the map repeatedly cited in the order was not found in the archive. The text therefore preserves recognition procedures and named objectives more securely than the complete graphic arrangement. It establishes intended cooperation, while the arrival and effect of supporting sorties require separate evidence.l

[10]

The comparison with Lithuania was already clear. In both regions, commanders tried to strike German flanks with corps whose assembly, communications and supplies were uncertain. Ukraine offered a larger and more sustained armoured response, but more tanks did not remove those constraints. Follow its continuation in The War Moves East.

Finland’s passage into open war

The northern war acquired another public turning point on 25 June when Soviet aircraft attacked targets in Finland. The American minister in Helsinki, H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, reported a late-afternoon conversation with Foreign Minister Rolf Witting in a dispatch sent at six. Witting said that Finland was again at war and that the government would make its position clear to the Diet that evening. He also emphasized that Finland was no longer alone; Schoenfeld understood his remarks as implying reliance on German assistance. The dispatch records the Finnish government’s immediate presentation of the attacks and the American envoy’s interpretation of its strategic position. [12]

The air attacks were a real escalation, but they did not create German–Finnish military cooperation out of nothing. German troops were already deployed in Finland, and preparations for operations against the Soviet Union had been coordinated before Barbarossa began. The Finnish leadership sought to recover territory lost in the Winter War and pursued its own national objectives, while the German command sought strategic benefits against the Soviet north. Those aims overlapped sufficiently to produce military cooperation without making Finland’s war identical in every respect to Germany’s. The distinction helps explain Finnish decision-making; it does not make the prior preparations disappear. [5]

The confrontation widened Soviet commitments across a northern theatre far beyond the Baltic advance. German and Finnish forces prepared separate operations against Murmansk, the railway farther south and the approaches to Leningrad. Their deployments and plans must be distinguished from offensives already under way on 25 June.[4]m

Conquest and murder in Kaunas

While Soviet units struggled to withdraw through Lithuania, Jews in Kaunas faced a danger for which the operational maps provide almost no adequate language. In his subsequent report covering the period to 15 October, Einsatzgruppe A commander Walter Stahlecker described efforts to encourage local anti-Jewish violence while concealing German direction. His account identified the night of 25–26 June as a major pogrom and credited a Lithuanian group led by Klimaitis with carrying it out after prompting from a German advance detachment. The report’s vocabulary attempted to turn murder into an administrative achievement. Its explicit concern with making German involvement invisible is particularly important evidence. [13]

Stahlecker’s account describes an effort to direct and conceal German participation, but it does not explain every local attack. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum documents violence against Jews by Lithuanian groups in the interval between the Soviet retreat and the German occupation of Kaunas on 24 June, followed by escalating persecution under German rule. Many Jewish inhabitants tried to flee east; refugees found the Soviet border closed. During the night of 25–26 June, attackers murdered Jews and burned homes in Slobodka, the predominantly Jewish neighbourhood across the river. The victims’ exposure resulted from several developments converging: flight obstructed, local violence already underway and German security units turning conquest into organized murder. Stahlecker’s self-serving totals should not be treated as a neutral census of those killed. [14] [13]

German propaganda and local antisemites turned anger at Soviet occupation into accusations against Jews collectively. The accusation was false. Families and communities were persecuted for their identity, not for acts established against them. The earlier Soviet repression explains part of the setting; it neither transfers responsibility for Soviet crimes nor excuses the murders that followed.[13]n

Evidence of concealment

A report that describes its own deception

Stahlecker described encouraging anti-Jewish attacks while making their origin appear local and hiding German direction. His report is evidence both of instigation and of an effort to disguise responsibility. Visible local participation therefore cannot, by itself, disprove German involvement.[13]o

These murders unfolded during the advance. Conquest gave German security detachments access to towns, collaborators and Jewish communities while fighting continued for the next crossings. The military and civilian histories intersected through that change in power, although the acts of persecution require their own identification of perpetrators and victims.

What the counterattacks changed

By 25 June, Soviet armour had checked individual German formations and forced hard fighting for particular routes. Those actions had not restored the front. Broken communications, missing units and fuel shortages prevented sustained, coordinated attacks, while German forces on other routes continued towards the crossings needed for Soviet withdrawal.[2]

The Soviet orders provide a concrete measure of the failure. Poluboyarov had sought coordinated attacks on 23 June; the Southwestern Front was still issuing renewed assignments for 26 June. The interval contained real fighting, but the intended converging blows had not produced their assigned result. German forces were still moving towards the crossings through which Soviet armies would have to retreat. Each unsuccessful counterstroke left less time to restore the connections needed for the next attempt. [1] [11] [5]

The counterattacks had imposed costs and interruptions without restoring the communications and freedom of movement needed for a coherent Soviet defence. In the central sector, those conditions were deteriorating on a still larger scale as German mobile forces approached Minsk and Soviet armies farther west sought routes out. The next study follows that transition from threatened withdrawal to encirclement. There, formations continued fighting even as the headquarters, communications and supply arrangements needed to sustain a common defence were breaking apart.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the passages used. Soviet documents are accessed in published transcriptions, not as original archive files; their archival references are those printed by the editors. Orders establish intended actions, while reports preserve contemporary estimates and gaps. German operational histories are read with their dependence on German records and postwar testimony in mind. Perpetrator documents are distinguished from neutral counts, and later recollections from contemporary testimony. Žardinskas’s article is used through its inspected English abstract; no uninspected tactical detail is attributed to the full article. Lettered evidence notes retain detailed references and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the source register below.
